subject: Computer Networking
title: Social Engineering
description: Learn Social Engineering in one minute.

hook.text: The strongest firewall in the world can't stop a human who clicks a bad link. People are the weakest point.

buildup.text: Social engineering tricks people into giving up passwords, access, or money through manipulation, not hacking.

discovery.text: Phishing emails look like they're from your bank. Pretexting calls sound like IT support. The disguises are convincing.

twist.text: Even tech companies fall for it. In 2020, a teen tricked Twitter employees into giving access to celebrity accounts.

climax.text: Training and awareness are the only defenses. Technology can flag suspicious messages, but judgment is the last line.

punchline.text: Hackers don't always hack computers. Sometimes they hack people.

quiz.question: What is social engineering in cybersecurity?
options: Manipulating people into revealing sensitive information

details.summary: Social engineering manipulates people into breaking security procedures by exploiting trust, authority, urgency, and helpfulness. Techniques include pretexting, baiting, tailgating, and impersonation.
details.whyItMatters: The most sophisticated technical security is useless if an attacker can convince an employee to bypass it. Social engineering exploits human psychology, the hardest vulnerability to patch.
takeaways: Social engineering exploits trust and human psychology, not technology
Pretexting creates false scenarios to manipulate targets
Security awareness training is the primary defense

faq.question: What are common social engineering techniques?
faq.answer: Pretexting creates a fabricated scenario to gain trust. Baiting offers something enticing like a USB drive with malware. Tailgating follows an authorized person through a secure door. Vishing uses phone calls impersonating IT support or executives. Each exploits a different aspect of human behavior.

faq.question: How do organizations defend against social engineering?
faq.answer: Regular security awareness training teaches employees to recognize manipulation techniques. Simulated phishing tests measure vulnerability and reinforce training. Clear procedures for verifying identity before granting access or sharing information create consistent defenses.
